An attacker can submit an arbitrary Python expression (e.g. `__import__('os').system('id')`) to the /evaluate endpoint and achieve full remote code execution on the server.

Shell metacharacters (e.g. `; id`, `$(...)`, `` ` ``, `|`) are not filtered, allowing arbitrary OS command injection.

extra.message: `rp()` executes any string passed to it via `os.popen(cmd)` without validation, running the command through the system shell. This is the sink for the command injection reachable from `/lookup`.

extra.message: User-supplied `request.form['name']` is embedded via `%` string formatting directly into the Jinja2 `template` string (lines 221-234), which is then rendered with `render_template_string()`. Because the user input becomes part of the template source itself (not just template data), an attacker can inject Jinja2 syntax such as `{{ config }}` or `{{ self.__init__.__globals__.__builtins__ }}` to achieve Server-Side Template Injection and typically Remote Code Execution.

extra.message: The `/xml` endpoint parses user-supplied XML (`request.form['xml']`) using `etree.XMLParser(no_network=False, dtd_validation=True)` and `etree.fromstring()`. Enabling DTD validation and network access allows processing of `<!DOCTYPE>`/`<!ENTITY>` declarations, including external entities, letting an attacker read local files (e.g. `file:///etc/passwd`) or trigger SSRF via crafted XML with external entity references.

extra.message: Login authenticates by querying `User.query.filter_by(username=name, password=passw)` — the plaintext password submitted by the user is compared directly against the plaintext value stored in the database. Combined with `register()` (line 62), which stores `request.form['password']` as-is with no hashing (see `password = db.Column(db.String(80))`, line 23), credentials are persisted and compared without any hashing/salting, so a database compromise or leak exposes all user passwords directly.

`app.debug = True` is set and the app is run bound to `host="0.0.0.0"` (line 242), exposing it on all network interfaces with Flask's debug mode enabled. Debug mode enables the Werkzeug interactive debugger, which can leak stack traces/source code and, if reachable and unprotected, allow arbitrary code execution through the in-browser debug console.
